atha caturtho vimarśaḥ | īśvaramaśeṣatāpapraśamanamamṛtadravaṃ sadā vande | apratighātisvecchāvikāsaviśrāntamamṛtakaramaulim || evaṃ jñānam, tataḥ smṛtiḥ, taddvayāntaḥprāṇikā apohanaśaktiriti yadyapi kramaḥ; tathāpi athānubhavavidhvaṃse smṛti ..................| (1|2|3) iti pūrvapakṣe satyaṃ kintu smṛtijñānaṃ ................. | (1|3|1) iti siddhānte smṛtireva pūrvaprakrāntā na cet iti sūtritena prasaṅgena sūcitāt prasaṅgaviparyayādātmeśvarasiddhau sātiśayamabhijñānam | ata eva gītāsu sā eva prathamamupāttā | tadasyāḥ svadarśane upapattirabhidhīyate sa hi pūrvānubhūtārthopalabdhā .................... | ityādinā .......................... arthau bhātaḥ pramātari || ityantena ślokāṣṭakena | anyathāhi kaścit brūyāt- māstu paradarśane smṛtirupapāditā, bhavaddarśane'pitu kathaṃ sā upapadyate iti | tatra ekena tadupapattiruktā | ekena smṛteranubhūtārthaprakāśanasāmarthyamuktam | (page 2) anyena anubhavatadviṣayābhyāmekatāparyanta āveśaḥ | turyeṇa smṛtāvanubhavo viṣayatayā pṛthak na bhātīti | yogijñānenāpi parānubhavo na pṛthaktayā viṣayavat prakāśyate iti bruvatā pañcamena tadartha eva draḍhitaḥ | anyena smṛtyā jñānasya pṛthagviṣayīkaraṇaṃ śaṅkyamānaṃ kālpanikaṃ, na vāstavamiti uktam | smṛtiprasaṅgena vikalpasya api anubhavena tādātmyaṃ saptamena uktam | antyena smartavyasmṛtismartṝṇāṃ prasaṅgataśca dṛśyadarśanadraṣṭṝṇāṃ pāramārthikaikasaṃvittattvaviśrāntirdarśiteti tātparyam | tatra prathamamupoddhātaḥ samastaśāstrārthapīṭhabandha ityabhiprāyeṇa āha avataraṇikāyām idānīṃ jñānaprakaraṇena iti | jñānaṃ smṛtyādirūpaṃ svadarśane ghaṭate ityevaṃ vicāryatvena prakriyate'dhikriyate'smin, tena | nirūpayiṣyan iti kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyāmupapade bhaviṣyati ḷṭ | tena ayamarthaḥ- smṛtyādīnāṃ sarveṣāṃ svarūpaṃ nirūpayiṣyāmīti hṛdaye gṛhītvā smṛtereva iti yasyāḥ pūrvopakrāntatā tasyā eva īśvaraśaktirūpatāṃ pratipādayitumicchan paradarśane sarvathaiva aghaṭamānatvamabhidadhat prathamaṃ pūrvaṃ saṃbhavamāha anena ślokena granthakṛt granthakṛdabhinna
**Memory as the Lord's power: how the "I" holds time together** The jñānādhikāra has established knowledge; now it takes up memory. And here Abhinavagupta makes a startling claim. The ordinary view — the view of the schools — is that memory is only the revival of an impression after the experience is gone. When the experience is destroyed, a mere trace remains, and memory is the stirring of that trace. But Abhinavagupta rejects this. Memory, he insists, is itself a *knowledge*; and far from being a pale echo of experience, it is the **Lord's own power** — the un-broken manifestation by which the past and the present are held together in the single "I." Consider what memory actually does. It brings the previously-experienced object back before the mind; the object appears, again, in the knower. If memory were only an impression's revival, this would be inexplicable — for how could a mere trace present an object? The truth is that memory is the un-broken manifestation of the experienced object: the experience and its object are carried forward into the memory as one. In memory, the experience does not stand apart as a separate object; it is the very act of knowing that returns. Even the yogin's knowledge of another, Abhinavagupta notes, does not appear as a detached object — it is the one awareness continuing. The separation that memory seems to make between the past cognition and the present one is only a construction (kālpanika), not a real division. And ultimately, the remembered, the memory, and the rememberer — and by the same token the seen, the seeing, and the seer — all rest in the one consciousness-essence. Now the "I" itself. The "aham" shines in two directions at once. As "the seer of the blue" it is turned inward; but the same "I, thus" is also turned outward toward the blue. The experience is the outward- facing blue-knowledge. And here is the freedom: by the freedom of the awareness, one first construes, within, "I would see the blue," and then the blue appears without. The inner construing precedes the outer manifestation, as the seed precedes the sprout. So the object, tinted by its place and its time, enters the knower and the experience together; and in the memory "I saw the blue then," the three — the I, the blue, the then — appear entered into that one act. This is the key to time itself. When we say "the jar stands, will stand, stood," what makes this possible is the un-brokenness of the manifestation — the awareness that holds the jar's appearances together across the moments. The experience is the gate through which time is entered. As long as the awareness is not touched by time, there is no time-dealing at all; but when it manifests the jar in its past, present, and future, time appears. And the one who says "I" across all of this is the same — the one self, who saw, who remembers, who will see. Memory is the thread by which the "I" holds time together, and it is, in the end, the Lord's own power shining as the un-broken awareness. ---
